items.prompt: What actually pushes a baby out during birth?

options.label: Powerful contractions of the uterus muscle
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: The baby swims out using its own limbs
options.feedback: A baby has no room or fluid current to swim through at this stage. It is moved, not swimming itself out.

options.label: The mother's diaphragm pushes down on it
options.feedback: Pushing with the diaphragm can help later on, but the force that opens the way and moves the baby along comes from elsewhere.

options.label: The placenta detaches and ejects the baby
options.feedback: The placenta usually separates only after the baby is already born, not before, and it does not act as an ejector.

items.ok_line: One muscle, working in waves, does the job.
items.ko_line: The baby has no way to move itself out — something around it has to do the work.
items.exp_text: The uterus is itself a large, thick muscle, and as labor begins it starts tightening and relaxing in waves called contractions. Each wave squeezes from the top downward, gradually opening the way and easing the baby toward the birth canal.

items.prompt: Why does a newborn need to cry or gasp right after birth?

options.label: To signal the mother that it is hungry
options.feedback: Hunger is not yet the issue in the first moments after birth. Something more urgent is happening in the lungs.

options.label: To clear fluid from its lungs and pull in its first breath of air
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: To stretch its lungs so they grow faster
options.feedback: Long-term lung growth is not what is happening in these first seconds. The lungs need to start working right away, not simply stretch.

options.label: To warm up its body
options.feedback: Crying is not a way of generating body heat. Warmth comes from other means entirely.

items.ok_line: That first cry clears the way for the first real breath.
items.ko_line: Think about what has filled the lungs up until this exact moment, and what needs to replace it.
items.exp_text: Inside the uterus a baby's lungs are filled with fluid rather than air, since there was never any air to breathe. The strong cry or gasp at birth forces that fluid out and draws in air, starting the lungs working on their own.

items.prompt: What happens to the place where the umbilical cord was attached?

options.label: It grows into a new organ
options.feedback: Nothing new grows there. The connection simply seals over once it is no longer needed.

options.label: It reattaches somewhere else on the belly
options.feedback: The cord's attachment point does not move to a different spot. It heals right where it was.

options.label: It heals over and becomes the navel
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: It stays open permanently
options.feedback: Left open, that spot would be vulnerable. It closes over instead, well before it stays that way forever.

items.ok_line: The scar of a supply line no longer needed.
items.ko_line: Ask what every person carries on their belly for the rest of their life, and where it comes from.
items.exp_title: A scar that stays for life
items.exp_text: Once the umbilical cord is cut, the short stump left on the baby's belly dries up and eventually detaches, and the skin underneath heals over the spot. That healed spot is the navel, a permanent mark of where the baby was once connected to the placenta.

items.prompt: Why does a newborn's skull have soft spots where the bone hasn't fully joined?

options.label: So the baby can hear better
options.feedback: Hearing does not depend on how the skull bones are joined. These soft spots serve a mechanical purpose instead.

options.label: So the brain can be examined easily
options.feedback: These spots exist for the baby's own development, not to make it easier for anyone else to look inside.

options.label: Because the bones haven't started forming yet
options.feedback: The bone plates have already formed by birth. What is missing is not the bone itself but the fixed joints between the pieces.

options.label: So the skull can be squeezed through birth and can keep growing afterward
options.feedback: Correct.

items.ok_line: Flexible now, for two good reasons.
items.ko_line: Think about the tight space the skull has to pass through, and the growing it still has ahead of it.
items.exp_title: Flexible plates, not one solid shell
items.exp_text: A newborn's skull is made of several separate bone plates with soft, flexible gaps between them, rather than one fused shell. Those gaps let the plates overlap slightly to fit through the birth canal, and afterward they let the skull keep expanding to make room for a rapidly growing brain.

items.prompt: What is the waxy white coating sometimes seen on a newborn's skin?

options.label: A protective coating that guarded the skin while it soaked in fluid for months
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: Dead skin that never got washed off before birth
options.feedback: This is not simply unwashed dead skin. It is a substance produced by the skin for a specific purpose during development.

options.label: A layer of fat for warmth
options.feedback: Warmth is provided by a different kind of fat stored elsewhere in the body, not by this coating on the skin's surface.

options.label: Leftover placenta tissue
options.feedback: It has nothing to do with the placenta. It is made by the baby's own skin.

items.ok_line: A waterproof coat, worn for months before birth.
items.ko_line: Think about what months spent surrounded by fluid would do to unprotected skin.
items.exp_title: A waterproof coat for months in fluid
items.exp_text: A baby's skin spends months surrounded by amniotic fluid, and without protection that soaking would soften and wrinkle it. The skin produces a waxy coating that shields it from the fluid, and traces of that coating can still be visible at birth.

items.prompt: Why does a newborn automatically curl its fingers tightly around anything placed in its palm?

options.label: It is copying a movement it saw
options.feedback: A newborn has had no chance to watch and copy this action. The grip happens without any such example.

options.label: It is an automatic reflex present from birth, not a learned action
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: Its muscles are too weak to let go
options.feedback: The grip is often surprisingly strong rather than a sign of weakness, and it is not a failure to release.

options.label: It is trying to communicate
options.feedback: The response happens automatically the instant something touches the palm, not as a deliberate signal to anyone.

items.ok_line: Built in from birth, not picked up afterward.
items.ko_line: A newborn has had no chance to learn this. Ask what a body can already do without being taught.
items.exp_title: A grip that needs no teaching
items.exp_text: Touching a newborn's palm triggers an automatic reflex wired into the nervous system before birth, closing the fingers without any thought or practice involved. That grasping reflex is present from the moment of birth and fades on its own as the following months pass.

items.prompt: Why does a newborn turn its head and open its mouth when its cheek is touched?

options.label: It is startled by the touch
options.feedback: This is a directed, repeatable response toward the touch, not a general startle away from it.

options.label: It is copying its mother's movements
options.feedback: A newborn shows this response to any light touch on the cheek, even from someone it has never seen move.

options.label: It is an automatic reflex that helps it find food
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: It is trying to see what touched it
options.feedback: The head turns toward the touch even with the eyes closed, so seeing the source is not what drives it.

items.ok_line: A built-in reflex aimed straight at feeding.
items.ko_line: Think about what this turning-and-opening response would help a newborn do right after birth.
items.exp_title: A reflex aimed at the next meal
items.exp_text: A light touch on a newborn's cheek triggers it to turn its head toward that side and open its mouth, a reflex called rooting. That automatic turning points the mouth toward a nearby breast, and it works alongside a matching sucking reflex once the mouth makes contact.

items.prompt: How does a newborn generate heat, since it cannot yet shiver effectively?

options.label: By moving its limbs constantly
options.feedback: A newborn's movements are not vigorous or constant enough to generate meaningful heat on their own.

options.label: By absorbing warmth stored in the placenta
options.feedback: The placenta is no longer connected after birth, so it cannot supply any warmth at this stage.

options.label: It cannot generate its own heat at all
options.feedback: A newborn is not helpless in this regard. It has a specific way of producing heat from within its own body.

options.label: By burning a special kind of fat that produces heat directly
options.feedback: Correct.

items.ok_line: A special fat, built for heat rather than storage.
items.ko_line: Shivering is not yet an option for a newborn — something else has to supply the heat instead.
items.exp_title: Fat built to burn for heat
items.exp_text: Before birth, a baby stores deposits of a special tissue called brown fat, packed with structures that release energy as heat rather than storing it. After birth, the newborn can burn that fat directly to warm itself, filling in for shivering until its muscles are strong enough to take over.

items.prompt: Why does a newborn's head sometimes look temporarily cone-shaped after a vaginal birth?

options.label: The soft, unfused skull bones overlapped slightly to fit through the birth canal
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: The baby's head grows unevenly in the womb
options.feedback: The shape at birth is not a growth pattern from the womb. It appears suddenly during the passage through the birth canal itself.

options.label: Forceps reshape it during delivery
options.feedback: Most births involve no instruments at all, yet this shape can still appear, so something else must explain it.

options.label: Swelling from crying causes it
options.feedback: The shape is usually already visible in the first moments, before any crying has had time to cause swelling.

items.ok_line: The same flexible plates that allow the squeeze also allow the shape.
items.ko_line: Think back to why a newborn's skull bones are not fully joined in the first place.
items.exp_title: A temporary squeeze, not a lasting shape
items.exp_text: Because a newborn's skull plates are not yet fixed together, they can slide over one another slightly as the head is squeezed through the narrow birth canal. That overlap can leave the head looking briefly cone-shaped, and it settles back to a more rounded shape within a few days as the plates shift apart again.

items.prompt: What happens to the short stump of umbilical cord left after birth?

options.label: It stays attached permanently
options.feedback: The stump is not a permanent fixture. It is tissue that is no longer supplied with blood and cannot stay attached.

options.label: It dries out and drops off on its own within a couple of weeks
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: It is absorbed back into the body
options.feedback: The stump does not get reabsorbed. Once cut, it has no blood supply left to keep it living tissue.

options.label: It turns into a scar immediately
options.feedback: The scar forms only after the stump has dried up and fallen away, not right at the start.

items.ok_line: No blood supply left, so it dries up and falls away.
items.ko_line: Ask what happens to any tissue once its blood supply is cut off.
items.exp_title: Tissue with nothing left feeding it
items.exp_text: Once the umbilical cord is clamped and cut, the short stump left behind no longer has any blood flowing through it. With nothing feeding it, the stump dries up, darkens and eventually drops away, leaving the healing navel behind.
